items.title: A shape with finite volume but infinite surface area
items.claim: Rotate y = 1/x for x at least 1 around the x-axis. You get a 'horn' extending to infinity. Its volume is exactly pi (finite). Its surface area is infinite. You could fill it with paint, but never paint its interior.
items.prompt: How can volume be finite if surface area isn't?

options.text: The horn cannot be constructed in reality
Volume integrates 1/x squared (which is summable), while surface integrates 1/x (which is not); the integrals are independent, and one can converge while the other diverges
Surface and volume are always proportional in finite shapes

items.reveal:
Volume: V = pi * integral from 1 to infinity of (1/x) squared dx = pi * [-1/x] from 1 to infinity = pi.

Surface area: A = 2 * pi * integral from 1 to infinity of (1/x) * sqrt(1 + 1/x to the fourth) dx, which is greater than 2 * pi * integral from 1 to infinity of dx/x = infinity.

Intuition: volume scales as the square of the radius, surface as the radius. As you stretch toward infinity, the cross-sectional radius decreases as 1/x — the square (volume per unit length) decreases as 1/x squared (summable), but the radius itself (surface per unit length) decreases as 1/x (the harmonic series, divergent).

The 'paint paradox': filling the horn with pi cubic units of paint coats the interior — even though the surface 'should' need infinite paint to cover. The resolution: a paint film of any finite thickness doesn't fit at the horn's far reaches, where the radius is arbitrarily small.
items.why: Geometric intuition equates surface area and volume scaling. They're separate integrals; convergence of one doesn't imply convergence of the other.

items.title: A bottle with no inside
items.claim: A normal bottle has an inside and an outside, separated by the bottle wall. The Klein bottle has no inside. There is only one surface — what looks like 'inside' is connected to 'outside' through the surface itself.
items.prompt: How is the Klein bottle different from a regular surface?

options.text: It's non-orientable — there is no consistent way to assign 'outward normals'; a left-handed walker traversing it can come back as right-handed
It's actually two surfaces glued together
Klein bottles only exist in imagination

items.reveal:
Klein constructed the bottle as a 2D analogue of the Möbius strip — but closed. To build one in 3D, you must let the bottle 'pass through itself' (a fake self-intersection). Properly, it lives in 4-dimensional space, where it has no intersection.

In rigorous terms: the Klein bottle is a non-orientable, closed 2-manifold with Euler characteristic 0. It cannot be embedded in 3D Euclidean space without self-intersection.

The Möbius strip (Möbius, 1858) is a 2D example with boundary: cut one open and you get a long strip; cut it in half lengthwise and you get a single longer Möbius strip, not two.

Non-orientable surfaces matter in physics (some condensed matter systems behave like Möbius strips), engineering (conveyor belt design uses Möbius topology to wear evenly), and cosmology (toy models of non-orientable universes have been considered, though our universe seems to be orientable).
items.why: 3D objects have an obvious inside and outside. Topology shows some 2D surfaces don't — the apparently obvious 'inside/outside' distinction is a special feature of orientable manifolds.

items.title: You cannot walk across all seven Königsberg bridges once
items.claim: Königsberg (now Kaliningrad) sat on two riverbanks and two islands connected by seven bridges. The town's puzzle: is there a route that crosses each bridge exactly once? Euler proved in 1735 that there isn't — and invented graph theory in the process.
items.prompt: What's the criterion for the puzzle to have a solution?

options.text: Bridges must be arranged in a circle
Every vertex (landmass) must have even degree (an even number of bridges), except possibly the start and end points; Königsberg has four landmasses, all of odd degree
Bridges must be the same length

items.reveal_title: Euler's 1735 paper — birth of graph theory
items.reveal:
Euler abstracted Königsberg to a 'graph': landmasses become vertices, bridges become edges. The puzzle asks for an 'Eulerian path' (a walk using every edge exactly once).

Euler proved: an Eulerian path exists if and only if at most 2 vertices have odd degree. (A circuit, starting and ending at the same vertex, requires every vertex to have even degree.)

Königsberg: north bank had 3 bridges, south bank 3, east island 5, west island 3. All four are odd. So no Eulerian path exists.

Euler's paper was the first to study a problem in what we now call topology — caring about connections, not distances. Graph theory grew into a major branch of mathematics: shortest paths, network flows, Internet routing, social networks, and more.

Two of Königsberg's bridges were destroyed in World War II; only three of the original seven remain. Today the puzzle has a valid Eulerian path.
items.why: Geometric puzzles often look like they need detailed measurement. Sometimes only the abstract topology matters — and Euler's degree condition makes the answer trivial once formalised.
